en: Her interest is to force the sun to acknowledge that it is not absolute. <1>(p. 792)</1>
At the same time, Isis does not wish to annihilate the sun. <1>(p. 792)</1>
Once named, power ceases to operate as pure natural presence and becomes invocable, delimitable and, therefore, obliged to answer for its acts. <1>(p. 792)</1>
In continuous consumption, the acquisition inaugurates a position in the ecosystem and not a delivery exhausted in an instant. <1>(p. 428)</1>
Enjoyment, here, does not appear as an accidental effect of a formally concluded contract, but as the material core of the consumer relationship. <1>(p. 717-718)</1>
The way the conflict is narrated changes, because attention shifts from the isolated event to the supply program. <1>(p. 788)</1>
In continuous consumption, the acquisition inaugurates a position in the ecosystem and not a delivery exhausted in an instant.<1>p. 428</1>

The more the reconstruction of the conflict depends on internal governance, the less reasonable it will be to demand from the consumer a detailed showing of facts whose documentary and technical support was never within their reach.<1>p. 736</1>
Loss no longer appears as an exceptional event and comes to be metabolized as part of the normal functioning of the system. <1>(p. 781)</1>

It is enough that it acts stably upon the ordinary interpretation of the experience and upon the user's willingness to bear friction, accept vague justifications, normalize losses and remain in the cycle of use even when enjoyment has already been functionally degraded. <1>(p. 781)</1>

It is a functional infrastructure that organizes how the user understands the problem submitted, trusts the answer received, incorporates it into their decision-making, reviews it, corrects it or reassesses it in the face of error, fluctuation or change in performance. <1>(p. 757)</1>

It depends on the continuity of the system, the relative stability of the interface, the maintenance of the conditions of access, the model for presenting answers, the warnings, the contextual limits, the memory or history mechanisms where they exist, and the private rules that structure the very field of use. <1>(p. 759)</1>
It describes entry into a regulated ecosystem of use, subject to conditioning, limitation and reorganization by private governance. <1>(p. 758)</1>

Platforms of this nature do not merely connect. They select, rank, highlight, hide, bring closer, delay, prioritize and reorganize the way in which the reality of the environment becomes perceptible to the user. <1>(p. 761)</1>
In both cases, the platform governs the environment of appearance. <1>(p. 762)</1>
Consumers do not choose in a vacuum, before a transparent and symmetrical universe of offers. They choose within a field the platform has already pre-interpreted. <1>(p. 762)</1>
What is provided, in functional terms, is a private infrastructure of economic possibility. <1>(p. 765)</1>

It is a matter of recognizing that the functional utility indispensable to the exercise of economic activity is offered, modulated and reconfigured by a private architecture that the subject does not control. <1>(p. 766)</1>

The legal test cannot be only whether the account remains active. It needs to be whether the partner's functional position in the environment remains substantially equivalent to the one that structured their legitimate expectation of earnings and continuity. <1>(p. 767-768)</1>
The service is valuable not only because it answers, but because it induces the user to treat the answer as a relevant point of orientation. <1>(p. 758)</1>

There may be informational noise when the architecture of the answer projects an appearance of safety, completeness or sufficiency incompatible with the real limits of the service. There may be functional opacity when the user cannot reconstruct, in minimally verifiable terms, why a given output was presented to them, to what extent there was a relevant change in the system's behavior or which elements of the environment conditioned the answer that guided their conduct. <1>(p. 759)</1>

There may also be acute evidentiary asymmetry when the functional impact of the service depends on history, interactional context, internal parameters or records that remain concentrated with the supplier. In these scenarios, the injury does not need to appear as a direct lie to be legally relevant. It is enough that the environment replaces legibility with a performance of trust, shifting to the user the cost of bearing error, review, oscillation or functional loss without adequate institutional trails of reconstruction. <1>(p. 759)</1>
When your account is blocked or banned, which means permanent expulsion, you also lose access to everything in it, including what you bought. The company…

If the account is terminated, access is lost not only to the “game”, but to the set of data and virtual content that structured the experience, in addition to the assertion that there is no refund in cases of just cause <1>(p. 375)</1>

In platform ecosystems, sanctions do not operate merely as a one-off disciplinary response to conduct attributed to the user. They can affect access, permanence, visibility, reputation, relational insertion and continuity of enjoyment. For this reason, they must be controlled by denser criteria than the mere formal existence of sanctioning power. They require verifiable reasoning, decisional coherence and intelligible avenues of contestation. <1>(p. 749)</1>

The relevant punishment is often not to expel, but to demote, because remaining inside, but less visible, less eligible and less recognizable, amounts to degrading the position of enjoyment and eroding the value that depended on commensurability and validation in circuit. <1>(p. 373)</1>

In games operated as a service, consumption decisions tend to be fragmented over time, mediated by return cycles, urgency signals, promises of progression, social comparison and incentives embedded in the very design of enjoyment. <1>(p. 494)</1>
The focus on minors thus works as an institutional trigger to make visible asymmetries of understanding and of capacity to contest in environments governed by architecture. <1>(p. 494)</1>
You paid more because the item was rare, a special edition or a last chance, and later it went back on sale for less, in another store or in another currency.…

When the platform sells an item at a high price under the promise of exclusivity, or presents exclusivity as a relevant attribute to justify price and spending, it incorporates this quality into the content of the offer and into the perceived utility of the object. <1>(p. 213)</1>

If, after a period, the same item reappears in an alternative store, in a special currency, in an aggressive promotion or at a significantly lower price, and if the temporal limitation of the exclusivity was not adequately and comprehensibly disclosed at the time of acquisition, there is a retroactive reconfiguration of the value delivered, with frustration of legitimate expectation and violation of transparency. <1>(p. 214)</1>

In immaterial goods, especially when their enjoyment is publicly visible, utility is inseparable from status, rarity and social recognition, which function as part of the acquired enjoyment bundle. <1>(p. 452)</1>

In platform-governed ecosystems, what the consumer keeps over time is not only functional access to a digital performance, but a position of enjoyment that incorporates history, memory, recognition, identity projection and practical continuity of presence in the environment. <1>(p. 534)</1>

Clause 2.3 of Riot's Terms of Service provides that, once the account is terminated, the user loses access to the account, the associated data, the game currency and the virtual content, without refund in cases of just cause, with the further possibility of cancellation of other accounts and of access to other services. The clause is valuable because it lays the problem bare: what is lost is not merely an isolated item, but the global position of enjoyment, the history, the inventory, the trajectory and the practical continuity of insertion in the ecosystem <1>(p. 540-541)</1>
What is lost, in these cases, is not only access, but biographical continuity objectified within the governed regime itself. <1>(p. 543)</1>

The strength of the criterion appears sharply in cases such as removals of relevant functionalities, nerfs that empty acquired utility, interface changes that disrupt ordinary use, redefinitions of rules that downgrade the equivalence of what was promised <1>(p. 637)</1>

The permanence of the item, the functionality, the account, the access or the feature does not, by itself, neutralize the emptying of the experience if the concrete role of the object is degraded, diverted or made substantially different from the one that justified the purchase. <1>(p. 730)</1>

Mutability, by itself, is not unlawful. The problem begins when it ceases to operate as a legitimate form of maintenance, improvement or adaptation of supply and starts to degrade, empty or divert, in a relevant way, the function that justified the acquisition and structured the legitimate expectation of enjoyment. <1>(p. 729)</1>

The right to exploit, terminate or reorganize economic activity is not to be confused with a supposed right to annihilate, without duties of transition, preservation or transfer, the functional enjoyment already stabilized in the consumer's sphere. <1>(p. 709)</1>

When the service becomes unavailable, it is not only access that fails, but the virtual content itself loses immediate usefulness, because the environment that makes it enjoyable stops operating. <1>(p. 409)</1>

Photographs, histories, libraries, contact networks, progressions, projected identities, reputational positions and long-term investments cannot be legally treated as residues without density merely because they are technically housed in someone else's infrastructure. <1>(p. 796)</1>

In more serious cases, especially when the platform acts at once as arbiter of the environment and as an economic agent with a stake in its results, the opacity of the ranking may also intersect with broader abusive practices and carry competition repercussions of its own. <1>(p. 764)</1>
You bought in-app currency with real money, like a game's coins or an app's credits, and now the same item costs more coins. The…

What is observed, however, in platform-governed immaterial consumption, is an inversion of logic. The supplier does not limit itself to competing within a market. It designs the very world of reference in which consumption takes place, controls catalog, visibility, rules of circulation, the practical unit of account and conditions of permanence, and then begins to exercise, simultaneously, functions analogous to those of a market and of a normative authority, defining on its own the level of prices and the pace of internal inflation. <1>(p. 179)</1>

The consumer no longer deals with a price that can be compared and audited in a straight line, and begins to deal with multiple internal grammars that require situational reading, because each currency “speaks” a different language. <1>(p. 397)</1>
The impact is not homogeneous in all its effects, but it is common in its matrix. <1>(p. 776)</1>
Collective redress is justified when the harmful source remains unitary, repeatable and incorporated into the ordinary functioning of the platform. <1>(p. 774)</1>

In platform environments, the harmful source may lie in the very design of the supply regime, so that the unity of the problem does not stem primarily from the empirical repetition of episodes, but from the permanence of a single, repeatable and functionally expansive structure producing loss, opacity and asymmetry. The injury, then, is not only plural. It is architectural. <1>(p. 774)</1>
You received an item as a gift through the game's official feature, and later it disappeared from your account because there was fraud somewhere along the way. When the fraud…

The second layer is the operational risk the supplier already knew about. Riot maintains, for more than one title in its portfolio, specific guidance on unauthorized charges, financial fraud and later disputes of transactions. These communications show that chargebacks and the misuse of payment methods were not an external, extraordinary or unforeseeable fact. This was an institutionally recognized operational risk, with internal procedures for investigation, refund and suspension. <1>(p. 610)</1>

In a specific official policy, the company states that a bank reversal authorizes suspension of the Riot Account until full reimbursement, and may even lead to a permanent ban for repeat cases, and it also extends the sanctioning effect to gift transactions, reaching not only the sender but also the recipient of the content. <1>(p. 612)</1>

The gifting feature did not operate on the margins of the platform, nor did it constitute a clandestine or intrinsically deviant practice. On the contrary, Riot itself presented it as a regular feature, integrated into the game client, subject to objective eligibility requirements, quantitative limits, regional restrictions and standardized sending flows. <1>(p. 610)</1>

The first family of these techniques is that of artificial scarcity and manufactured urgency. Its mechanism is well known. Short windows, accelerated rotation of offers, countdown timers, “limited editions”, ephemeral events and temporary benefits are used to shift the decision from the field of rational comparison to that of reactive response. <1>(p. 670)</1>

In digital objects, the marginal cost of reproduction tends to fall drastically and, in theory, availability could expand without requiring productive capacity comparable to the factory, logistics and the extraction of inputs. Therefore, when a persistent regime of unavailability, exclusivity and last chance is observed in these markets, one is not facing a natural condition of the object, but a deliberate institutional choice, so that scarcity appears not as a fact, but as a project. <1>(p. 209)</1>

The supplier emphasizes urgency, benefit, rarity or prestige, but relegates to side conditions what really defines the substance of enjoyment, such as relevant limitations of use, the ordinary mutability of the object, equivalence parameters, possible losses, restricted windows of use, additional requirements for fulfilling the promise or specific conditions for maintaining the advertised value. <1>(p. 631)</1>

The platform's private sovereignty, in other words, no longer governs only the game and begins to contest the minimum conditions of reliability of the user's own machine. Under the vocabulary of security, this expansion usually appears as if it were mere technical inevitability. But the discourse of security does not, by itself, neutralize the legal relevance of the architecture adopted. <1>(p. 522)</1>
When protection of the IOC's competitive environment comes to depend on software loaded at kernel level, that is, on the deepest and most privileged layer of the operating system <1>(p. 521)</1>
The problem becomes one of proportionality, necessity, transparency and justifiability of the degree of technical interference required of the consumer. <1>(p. 523)</1>
The legally relevant promise is not always concentrated in a single statement. <1>(p. 725)</1>

Whenever enjoyment is preceded by curated cycles of anticipation, promise, suggested scarcity, symbolic distinction or insinuated equivalences, advertising will materially be part of the offer. <1>(p. 744-745)</1>

Control of the offer must fall on what was promised as value and as function, on what was concealed as cost, limitation or condition of precariousness, and on the correspondence between this semiotic frame and the real enjoyment made available to the consumer. <1>(p. 725)</1>

The more the reconstruction of the conflict depends on internal governance, the less reasonable it will be to require from the consumer a detailed demonstration of facts whose documentary and technical support was never within their reach. This does not eliminate the need for plausibility, argumentative sequencing or delimitation of the disputed object. <1>(p. 736)</1>

In IOCs, the supplier controls not only the object and the environment; it also controls the institutional memory of supply. It knows what was shown, when it was shown, how it was altered, which version was in force, which interface trail led to the contract, which parameter was applied in a sanction, which transaction occurred and in what technical context. When all these elements remain under the platform's monopoly, governance of the service also becomes governance of proof. <1>(p. 658)</1>
In environments of governed enjoyment, verifiability is part of the very duty to shape the relationship legitimately. <1>(p. 735)</1>
In platform-governed ecosystems, the conflict does not begin when the user decides to litigate, complain or formalize dissatisfaction. In many cases, it is governed before that. <1>(p. 780)</1>

The platform may, for example, offer a sense of transparency without delivering real intelligibility, produce an impression of listening without opening effective paths of contestation, mobilize a human tone without assuming proportional duties of reasoning or justification and distribute signs of care that work less as adequate information and more as semiotic cushioning of criticism. <1>(p. 782)</1>

What matters is not whether the user “felt” more or less welcomed, but whether the platform structured signs, routines and protocols capable of shifting the reading of the loss, reducing the critical force of the experience and weakening the probability of intelligible contestation. <1>(p. 782)</1>
On a social network, what you see and how many people see what you post, known as your reach, depend on the platform's own rules. When reach drops…

Functional equivalence, in turn, applies when changes to the intermediation regime, the visibility logic, the reputational criteria or the circulation rules significantly degrade the utility legitimately incorporated into the relationship, without compatible restoration. This can occur both in e-commerce and in the social circulation of content, whenever the platform substantially changes the functional role of the infrastructure it offered as an environment of exchange, reach or recognition. <1>(p. 764)</1>

Whenever access, permanence, visibility or contestation are conditioned by opaque sanctions, selective frictions, excessive costs of reaction or asymmetric reversal mechanisms, there will be an indication of abusive governance of the bond. <1>(p. 746)</1>

Informational inadequacy may thus take the form of excess, dispersion and flow architecture. Excess, when textual overload makes it impractical to distinguish the essential from the accessory. Dispersion, when the relevant elements of the relationship are fragmented across multiple documents, screens and paths without sufficient integration. <1>(p. 722)</1>
The decisive point, therefore, is not to prove that “the text was there”, but to assess whether the legally relevant meaning was knowable in real terms. <1>(p. 601)</1>

The legally relevant question is no longer whether a given piece of information was somewhere in the supplier's documentary ecosystem. It becomes whether that information was made accessible, comprehensible and relevant at the moment it could influence the legitimate formation of the consumer's expectation or reaction. <1>(p. 723)</1>
You think about quitting the game, the network or the service, but leaving means losing your rank, your reputation, your history and the ties that only exist in there. That…

Permanence comes to depend on continuous alignment with mutable operational standards, and leaving is no longer simple substitution of a service, because it involves a discontinuity of prestige, comparability and belonging. This dependence on administered recognition is legally relevant because it makes integrity and identity governed variables of enjoyment and requires, on the dogmatic plane, reinforced duties of qualified transparency, contestability, auditability and restoration proportional to the type of power exercised by the Lex Plataformae. <1>(p. 358-359)</1>

The exit barrier can be described as a form of social death within the ecosystem. The expression does not operate as moral dramatization, but as a functional description of the effect produced when the platform concentrates the records that sustain belonging and relevance, that is, history, repertoire, ranked position, signs of prestige, community ties and traces of participation. Leaving the environment, under these conditions, is not like migrating from one service to another, because it implies interrupting one's own socially recognizable existence in that world, with loss of symbolic continuity and practical erasure of marks of trajectory that have become a condition of public commensurability. <1>(p. 359)</1>

In captive contracts, the so-called supervening “consent” is often nothing more than forced adherence to the new state of affairs, especially when the consumer is already invested in the relationship and depends on the ecosystem to keep enjoying what they acquired. <1>(p. 654-655)</1>

The reduction rarely appears as an explicit cut of “classes”, but it may manifest as loss of reach, persistent downgrading of performance, cumulative restriction of functionalities, compression of limits, reordering of visibility or structural changes that raise the cost of enjoying the same utility. The logic is the same. The label and the price are kept, and the delivery of value is downgraded. <1>(p. 480)</1>
In less pompous and more useful language: it is not enough to leave the shell of the relationship intact if the content enjoyed has been hollowed out. <1>(p. 651)</1>
The trigger is not any minor change, any visual touch-up or any marginal fluctuation typical of the normal life of the service. <1>(p. 651)</1>
You paid, the button said buy, and the contract calls what you received a license, which is a permission to use that can be withdrawn. The name the contract…

Whenever the consumed utility depends structurally on an environment administered, modulated and made mutable by private governance, with impact on access, permanence, intelligibility or updating of the experience, the field of application of the IOC will be established. <1>(p. 743)</1>
The law does not condition the product on corporeality, nor tie it to the image of the tangible thing delivered once and for all. <1>(p. 574)</1>

Unlike a stage of the game, whose rules exist so that the player can, in theory, beat them, the game embedded in the consumer relationship is designed and refereed by the supplier itself, which defines the probabilities, sets the unit of account, recalibrates the internal exchange rate and establishes the deadlines, systematically reserving for itself the position of the house. <1>(p. 449)</1>

The point of greatest sensitivity arises when monetization relies on random mechanisms for obtaining items, often referred to in public debate as loot boxes. In these cases, the utility and value of what was acquired come to depend on internal distribution regimes, availability criteria and limits set by the platform, and are also tied to signals of scarcity, time windows and rarity regimes that make decisions more dependent on anticipation, urgency and expectation. <1>(p. 494)</1>

The platform organizes access to demand, distribution of calls, minimum predictability of pay, permanence in the productive flow, reputational criteria, prioritization patterns, acceptance rules and sanction mechanisms. <1>(p. 765)</1>

Changes to request distribution criteria, pricing parameters, eligibility rules, incentive models or reputational weights may preserve the program's name, the appearance of partnership and even the formal existence of the account, while substantially draining the economic utility that justified joining and sustained the continuity of productive enjoyment. <1>(p. 767)</1>
The existence of an economic interest on the part of the user does not, in itself, eliminate the vulnerability arising from the governance of the ecosystem. <1>(p. 779)</1>
The platform does not need to formally expel a competitor in order to restrict its competitiveness. <1>(p. 770)</1>

The peripheral professionalized user does not automatically become the strong party to the relationship just because their activity has an economic purpose. In all these cases, the legally relevant question lies in the density of the platform's governance over their insertion in the ecosystem. If permanence, the intelligibility of the environment, the reconstruction of the conflict and the challenge of relevant decisions remain concentrated under the platform's private control, the a priori exclusion of the CDC by formal label loses its footing. <1>(p. 778)</1>
What you built on a platform is an asset, even without a body.
Anyone who sells in an online store, works through an app or builds a client network inside another company's system can also lose what they built.
You have the asset, but you do not control the conditions for using what you have, and that is where the problem lies.
Ra, the Sun god, reigned over everyone, but he was not invulnerable.
Isis did not want to destroy the Sun. She only wanted him to acknowledge that he was not absolute.
Once named, power stops being pure presence, something that is simply there, and can be called upon, delimited and made to answer for what it does.
The first path is usually the company itself, through the customer service channel it offers.
Each path opens the chance for the company to respond, for someone outside to look at the case and for the law to be applied, but the result depends on the evidence and on each situation.
It helps to bring dated screenshots, screen recordings and the purchase, acceptance and confirmation screens.
When what you buy only exists inside a platform, the sale does not end at the click.
The company keeps maintaining, changing and controlling what you use, and that is why it holds duties that follow the purchase for as long as it lasts.
What changes is the way of telling the conflict, which stops being a loose episode and becomes the way the platform supplies what it sold.
This trust does not arise on its own from good service. It is often produced, adjusted and maintained by the design of the screen and of customer service.
On platforms, trust is not a spontaneous by-product of the good performance of the service. Frequently, it is produced, calibrated and maintained by design. <1>(p. 781)</1>
In a service you use every day, small frustrations get absorbed and stop looking like a problem. They start to look like the normal functioning of the system.
You enter an environment governed by the company's rules, policies and guidelines, which it can change, limit and reorganize whenever it wants.
What matters is that everything you need to work is offered, adjusted and changed by a system you do not control.
You used an artificial intelligence assistant, the program that converses, summarizes and guides, and the answer turned out to be wrong or the service started to work differently.
There may be a problem when it looks more certain and complete than the service really is.
It may be enough that it trades clarity for an appearance of reliability and leaves you with the cost of the error, the review or the loss.
What is required is that the penalty have a reason that can be checked, consistency between one decision and the next and an understandable path to challenge it.

Often the account stays active, but becomes less visible, loses rewards and has its chat cut off, and that also takes value from what you bought, because staying inside in a worse position is already a loss.
It comes in pieces, pulled along by return cycles, urgency notices, promises of progress, comparison with friends and incentives built into the game itself.
The law already sees children and teenagers as an audience that calls for special care in these environments, and there are specific rules on what can be offered to them.
They can reach the family, which comes to need more attention and may see its income affected.

The effects radiate over the family, generating expenses with treatments, demanding greater attention from those responsible and interfering with family income <1>Torres</1><2>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 23-24)</2>. <3>(p. 673)</3>
It may have come back in an alternative store, in a special currency or in a deep promotion.
In an item others can see, status, rarity and recognition are part of what you acquired.
What stays in the account over the years is not only access, but history, memory, recognition and the place you hold there.
A ban, which is the permanent expulsion from the account, a progress reset or a deletion took away years of history, inventory, achievements and reputation.
This loss can go beyond the price of what you bought, because the continuity of your own story in that environment goes with it.
The typical case is the item that remains in the inventory, with the same name, but became far too weak.
The item is still there, but it no longer works the same way, and what matters is whether the change took from it the role that justified the purchase.
An update, which is the change the company makes to the program after the sale, altered what you bought.
It can close the business, but that right does not include erasing everything without any care for those who were inside.
What you bought only works while someone keeps the servers on and the environment standing.
Photos, histories, libraries, contacts, progress, reputation and years of investment go with it, and they do not become worthless just because they are stored in another company's structure.
In an online store with many sellers, the so-called marketplace, you choose among what the platform put up front, with the badges, ratings and highlights it organizes.
It chooses what appears first, what stays hidden, who looks trustworthy and what can be compared.
When the same company arranges the shop window and also profits from what happens in it, the situation becomes more serious.

Riot does not describe the game currency as a simple neutral means of exchange. It treats it as part of a closed circuit, whose equivalence can be recalibrated unilaterally. The term admits that, “sometimes”, the company may alter the purchasing power of the Game Currency, including by increasing the number of coins needed to acquire virtual products such as skins, and places this movement under the generic promise of notice and progressiveness <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. <3>(p. 176)</3>
The company that sells the currency is the same one that sets the prices inside, and that is why the change must be looked at carefully.
Each currency works like a language of its own, and the one who has to translate everything is you.
The same problem hit many people in the same service, and each person stayed on their own side, thinking it was bad luck.
The cases do not need to be identical, because what repeats is the source of the problem.
The sign is a single origin, which repeats and is part of the normal way the service works.
What is usually behind it is the chargeback, which happens when someone disputes the card purchase and the bank reverses the payment.
It matters a lot whether the feature was official.
The countdown, the limited edition or the notice that the item was about to disappear made you decide quickly, perhaps before understanding everything you were buying.
A digital item could be sold to everyone, at any time, without running out.
The urgency is put in the spotlight, while the limits of use, the chance that the item changes and the possible losses are left in a corner.
Fighting cheating is legitimate, but the word security does not end the discussion about how far the company may rule over your machine.
It starts when the computer starts, and the company can block the game if it is turned off or removed.
The question is whether that interest is enough for the company to gain so much power over your equipment without stronger oversight.
The offer is what the company commits to deliver when it advertises.
You bought after seeing previews, countdowns, rarity badges or promises of prominence, and what arrived afterwards does not match what all of that led you to expect.
A loose, enthusiastic sentence with no weight in your decision is not enough.
That is why the work of proving can be divided according to each party's access, without relieving you of telling coherently what you went through.
The company knows what it showed you, when it showed it, which version was in force, which transaction took place and which rule it used in a penalty.
When all of this stays only with the company, whoever controls the service also comes to control the evidence.
Customer service is kind, answers quickly and asks you to wait, but the problem goes on, and you end up letting it go.
The answer seems to explain, but does not say what happened, and the tone is friendly, but no path to challenge it opens.
It is whether customer service works in a way that diverts the reading of the loss and drains the strength of your complaint.

Meta's Terms of Service describe an environment in which the use of Facebook is subject to private rules of permanence, visibility, sharing, moderation and organization of circulating content, so that the user's experience is mediated by internal criteria of distribution and management of social interaction <1>FACEBOOK</1><2>(Facebook, [202-?])</2>. <3>(p. 762)</3>
There may be a problem when the change affects the logic of visibility, the reputation criteria or the circulation rules.
Your access, your permanence, your visibility and your chance to complain may depend on penalties nobody explains.
There may be too much text, so that the essential gets lost among the rest, or the rule may be scattered across documents, screens and menus that do not connect.
Being written somewhere is not enough, because what counts is whether, at the moment of deciding, you had a way to understand what that rule meant.
Here it is different, because the history, the rank, the signs of prestige and the bonds you made stay with the company and are only worth anything inside.
The clearest sign appears when the company changes the rules and you accept only because leaving would cost more.
The name and the price stayed the same, and what shrank was the delivery.
The shell of the service can stay intact while its content has been emptied.
A one-day fluctuation or a small adjustment is not enough, and not every reduction is unlawful.

The Terms of Service describe the same items as “Virtual Content” offered under an access license tied to the account <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. The consequence is that what the interface presents as a “purchase”, the contractual instrument requalifies as conditioned and institutionally administered access. <3>(p. 401)</3>
It is how much what you use depends on an environment the platform maintains, adjusts and can change.
The name the contract gives does not alone decide your protection, because consumer law also treats as a product what has no body.
This is one of the most sensitive points of consumption in games, because the one who decides the odds, the currency, the rarity and the deadlines is the company itself.
The value of what you get comes to depend on internal rules of distribution, availability and rarity that only the company sets, often together with time windows and signs of scarcity.
When direct purchase disappears and the draw becomes mandatory, you stop choosing how to reach the item and start paying to try.

This design makes explicit a relevant loss of consumer autonomy, as the consumer no longer chooses the means of access to the good and starts to “pay to try”, with accumulated progression and a foreseen spending cap, in a logic that is only completed through continued consumption within the system itself <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024a)</2>. <3>(p. 450)</3>
You work making deliveries or rides through an app and, after a rule change nobody explained, the calls dropped, your earnings fell or a restriction arrived.
The one who distributes the calls, calculates the earnings, gives the rating, decides the priority and applies the restrictions is the app.
Even so, they can substantially empty the earnings that justified staying.
Earning income through the platform does not, by itself, remove that protection.
Those who sell depend on the ranking, the reputation and the prominence the platform controls.
What weighs is how much the platform governs your presence on it.
